title: Boundaries, Part 2: A Hard Question and Common Traps

beats.say: In part one, we learned to find the boundary, and to ask whether each side is an independent clause.
beats.item: Is each side an independent clause?

beats.say: Two independent clauses need a period or a semicolon, and extra information needs matching marks on both sides.
In this video, we work through a hard question with a colon and a conjunctive adverb, and then the common traps.
beats.item: Today: a hard question and traps

beats.say: Hard question. Words like however, therefore, and for example are not conjunctions. Between two independent clauses, they need a semicolon or a period before them.
A colon must follow a complete independent clause. If the words before the colon cannot stand alone, a colon is wrong.

card.text: A colon needs a full clause first

scenes.title: Read the sentence
scenes.text: The committee expected the new bridge to ease traffic on Main Street ______ however, drivers reported longer delays during the first month.

beats.say: The part before the blank is a complete sentence. The committee expected the new bridge to ease traffic.
The part after the blank begins with however, but still holds a full clause. Drivers reported longer delays. So both sides are independent.

scenes.title: Which punctuation fits?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

beats.say: Choice A uses only a comma before however. Between two independent clauses, that is a comma splice.
Choice B uses a colon. The second clause does not explain the first, it contrasts with it, so a colon does not fit.
Choice D uses no mark at all, so the two independent clauses run together.
Choice C uses a semicolon, with a comma after however. That correctly joins the two clauses. The answer is C.
Now the traps. Each one is a way that a careful reader can still pick a wrong answer. We will see the trap, and then the habit that avoids it.
Trap one. Extra information that opens with a comma, but closes with a dash, is mismatched. The marks must be the same on both sides.
beats.wrong: The mill, built in 1782— still runs

beats.say: Use two commas, or use two dashes. Never use one of each, because the pair must match.
beats.right: The mill, built in 1782, still runs

beats.say: Trap two. A comma before however, between two independent clauses, is a comma splice. However is not a conjunction.
beats.wrong: It was late, however, they stayed

beats.say: Use a semicolon or a period before however, and put a comma after it.
beats.right: It was late; however, they stayed

beats.say: Trap three. A colon needs a full independent clause before it. The words the recipe needs are not a full clause on their own.
beats.wrong: The recipe needs: flour and eggs

beats.say: Finish the clause first, and then use the colon to introduce the list.
beats.right: The recipe needs two items: flour, eggs

beats.say: Trap four. A semicolon works like a period, so both sides must be independent. A clause starting with which is dependent.
beats.wrong: He grew the plant; which flowers

beats.say: Use a comma before which, or fix the words so that both sides can stand alone.
beats.right: He grew the plant, which flowers

beats.say: Trap five. A comma between a subject and its verb is always wrong, even when the subject is long.
beats.wrong: The result of the study, was clear

beats.say: Remove the comma. Subject and verb stay together, with no mark in between.
beats.right: The result of the study was clear

beats.say: To recap. Use a semicolon before however between two clauses, and a colon only after a full clause.
beats.item: Semicolon before however; full clause before colon

beats.say: Match the marks around extra information, and never split a subject from its verb. In the next topic, we study form, structure, and sense.
